topic: Characteristics of the Indian Economy & Development

items.title: Economic Growth vs Economic Development
items.body:
**In one line:** Economic growth means the economy produces more (a bigger income), while economic development means that larger income also makes people's lives better — less poverty, less inequality, better health and education.

**Why it is asked:** Examiners test whether you can see that a rising GDP alone is not progress; 'growth versus development' underlies most Economy answers and several tricky MCQs.

## Two related but distinct ideas

- **Economic growth** = a sustained rise in a country's **real per-capita income / output** over a long period. It is a **narrow, quantitative** measure — 'more of the same output'.
- **Economic development** is **multidimensional and qualitative**: growth *plus* reduction of **poverty, inequality and unemployment**, a change in the **composition of output**, and improvements in health, education, nutrition and welfare.

| Feature | Economic Growth | Economic Development |
|---|---|---|
| Concept | Narrow | Comprehensive |
| Change | Quantitative | Quantitative + qualitative |
| Focus | More output/income | Output mix + welfare + equity |
| Ills tackled | Not addressed directly | Poverty, inequality, unemployment |

- Growth is **necessary but not sufficient** for development: 'jobless growth' or highly unequal growth raises GDP without improving lives.
- India is often described as showing **'jobless growth'**: in several years output (GDP) grew rapidly while employment generation lagged, especially in the organised sector. The second fact explains the first.
- **Inclusive growth** — growth whose benefits reach all regions, sectors and social groups — is the bridge between the two and a stated goal of Indian planning.

## Don't confuse

**Growth vs development:** growth is a number going up (real per-capita income); development is that growth *plus* a better quality and spread of life. All development includes growth, but not all growth brings development.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- Economic growth = long-run rise in real per-capita income; narrow and quantitative.
- Economic development = growth + reduction of poverty, inequality and unemployment; multidimensional and qualitative.
- Growth is necessary but not sufficient for development.
- Inclusive growth spreads benefits across regions, sectors and social groups.
- Jobless growth = GDP rises but employment lags, especially in the organised sector.
keyPoints: Economic growth = long-run rise in real per-capita income; narrow and quantitative.
Economic development = growth + reduction of poverty, inequality and unemployment; multidimensional and qualitative.
Growth is necessary but not sufficient for development.
Inclusive growth spreads benefits across regions, sectors and social groups.
Jobless growth = GDP rises but employment lags, especially in the organised sector.
items.mnemonic: Growth = 'how MUCH'; Development = 'how GOOD' (composition + welfare + equity).
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Indian Economics: Growth and Development

items.title: Features of India as a Developing, Mixed Economy
items.body:
**In one line:** India is a developing, mixed economy — still poor per head, part-modern and part-traditional, heavily dependent on agriculture for jobs, and run by both private firms and the state.

**Why it is asked:** These structural features are the standard checklist APPSC uses to describe the nature of the Indian economy.

## Structural characteristics

- **Low per-capita income** — India remains a **lower-middle-income** economy (nominal per-capita income ~US$2,750 — IMF, April 2026), far below advanced economies.
- **Economic dualism** — a **modern** sector (IT, organised industry, finance) coexists with a large **traditional/subsistence** sector (small farms, informal trades).
- **Agrarian dependence** — agriculture still employs roughly **44–46%** of the workforce though it yields under a fifth of output.
- **Overpopulation & dependency** — a large population with a still-significant dependency burden, though the age structure now favours a demographic dividend.
- **Demographic dividend** — the faster growth potential an economy gets when the share of its **working-age (15–59) population** rises, because more people earn and fewer depend on them. It is a chance, not a guarantee: it needs jobs, skills and health.
- **Capital deficiency** — low per-capita capital and low (though rising) rates of savings and capital formation. Even a high-saving economy may not raise output much if the **capital-output ratio (ICOR) is high** — i.e. more units of investment are needed per extra unit of output (inefficient capital use).
- **Mass poverty, unemployment and underemployment**, including **disguised unemployment** in agriculture.
- **Dominance of the informal/unorganised sector** in employment.

## Mixed economy

- **Public and private sectors coexist** with a role for state planning — the model India adopted after 1947, liberalised progressively since **1991**.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- India is a lower-middle-income economy; nominal per-capita income ~US$2,750 (IMF, 2026).
- Economic dualism: modern sector coexists with a large traditional/subsistence sector.
- Agriculture employs ~44–46% of workers but contributes under a fifth of GVA.
- Capital deficiency, mass poverty, unemployment/underemployment and disguised unemployment persist.
- Mixed economy = public + private sectors with state planning; liberalised since 1991.
keyPoints: India is a lower-middle-income economy; nominal per-capita income ~US$2,750 (IMF, 2026).
Economic dualism: modern sector coexists with a large traditional/subsistence sector.
Agriculture employs ~44–46% of workers but contributes under a fifth of GVA.
Capital deficiency, mass poverty, unemployment/underemployment and disguised unemployment persist.
Mixed economy = public + private sectors with state planning; liberalised since 1991.

items.title: Sectors of the Economy & Structural Transformation
items.body:
**In one line:** Economists split the economy into layers — primary, secondary, tertiary and beyond — and India's unusual shift straight from farming to services, skipping a strong manufacturing phase, is the headline fact.

**Why it is asked:** Sector shares, the Eight Core Industries list, and the real-versus-financial and fixed-versus-working capital distinctions are frequent, factual MCQ targets.

## Classification by activity

- **Primary** — direct use of natural resources: agriculture, fishing (in rivers or coastal waters), forestry, mining. Turning sugarcane into sugar in a mill is **secondary**, because a raw material is processed.
- **Secondary (industrial)** — transforms raw materials into goods: manufacturing, construction.
- **Tertiary (services)** — supports production: transport, banking, IT, education, healthcare.
- **Quaternary** — knowledge/information services (R&D, IT, consulting).
- **Quinary** — top-level decision-making and policy ('gold-collar').

## Classification by ownership / regulation

- **Public vs private** — by ownership and objective (welfare vs profit).
- **Organised vs unorganised (informal)** — by regulation and social protection; the **informal sector dominates employment** (~80–90% of workers).

## Structural transformation (current shares)

| Sector | GVA share (approx.) | Workforce share |
|---|---|---|
| Services | ~54.7% | ~30% |
| Industry | ~27.6% | ~25% |
| Agriculture | ~17.7% | ~44–46% |

- Over the decades the **share of agriculture in GVA has declined** while the **services share has risen**.
- India shifted **agriculture → services**, largely **skipping a strong manufacturing phase** and leaping to a services-led structure — an unusual transition.
- **Don't confuse:** the fall in agriculture's GVA share has **NOT** been matched by an equal fall in its workforce share — people left farming far more slowly than output did.
- The **gap** between agriculture's low GVA share and its high workforce share signals **low productivity** and disguised unemployment.
- **Index of Eight Core Industries** covers coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilizers, steel, cement and electricity — combined weight **~40.27% of the IIP** under the 2011-12 series (the IIP/ICI are being rebased to **2022-23**, new IIP series released 1 June 2026). **Refinery products has the highest weight (~28%)**, followed by electricity and steel; **textiles and automobiles are NOT core industries**. (Refinery products = petroleum products such as petrol, diesel and LPG.)

## Real vs financial sector; fixed vs working capital

- **Real sector** = actual production of goods/services (farming, manufacturing); **financial sector** = money/credit flows (bank lending, issuing bonds). A farmer harvesting a paddy crop and a textile mill converting cotton into fabric are real-sector; a bank lending to a trader and a company issuing rupee bonds overseas are financial-sector.
- **Fixed capital** = durable assets used repeatedly (machinery, computer, a farmer's plough); **working capital** = inputs used up in one use (raw materials, petrol/fuel, yarn a weaver weaves into cloth).

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- Primary (natural resources), Secondary (manufacturing), Tertiary (services); plus Quaternary (knowledge) and Quinary (decision-making).
- Current GVA shares: Services ~54.7%, Industry ~27.6%, Agriculture ~17.7%.
- Agriculture's workforce share (~44–46%) far exceeds its GVA share — low productivity.
- Eight Core Industries ~40.27% of IIP (2011-12 series; rebased to 2022-23, June 2026); refinery products has the highest weight; textiles is NOT a core industry.
- Real sector = production (farming, manufacturing); financial sector = bank lending, bond issue.
- Fixed capital = durable (machinery, computer, plough); working capital = used-up inputs (petrol, yarn, raw materials).

items.title: National Income Aggregates & Measurement
items.body:
**In one line:** This is the quick reference for how GDP, GNP, NNP and National Income connect, and how output is actually measured.

**Why it is asked:** The aggregates and their conversions are the most formula-tested part of the Economy syllabus; the dedicated National Income notes carry the fully worked numerical examples.

## Key aggregates

- **GDP** = value of all final goods and services produced **within a country's territory** in a year.
- **GNP = GDP + NFIA** (Net Factor Income from Abroad) — output by **nationals** wherever located.
- If NFIA is **negative** (foreigners earn more in India than Indians earn abroad), **GNP is smaller than GDP**; if NFIA is positive, GNP is larger.
- **NDP = GDP − Depreciation** (GDP minus depreciation); **NNP = GNP − Depreciation**.
- **NNP at factor cost = National Income**.
- **Per-capita income = National Income ÷ Population** (national income divided by population).

## Valuation adjustments

- **Market price → Factor cost**: subtracting indirect taxes and adding subsidies.
- **Nominal GDP** = valued at current market prices (can rise merely due to inflation); **Real GDP** = valued at constant base-year prices, so it better reflects genuine output change — it is GDP adjusted for inflation using a base year (India's base year: **2022-23**, new series from Feb 2026).
- **GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP) × 100**.

## Three methods of estimation

| Method | Adds up |
|---|---|
| Production / value-added | GVA of each industry (output − intermediate consumption) |
| Income | Wages + rent + interest + profit |
| Expenditure | C + I + G + (X − M) |

- **GVA at basic prices** is now headlined alongside GDP at market price; GDP(mp) = GVA + net product taxes.
- **MoSPI / NSO (CSO)** compiles the National Accounts; the first estimate of Indian national income was by **Dadabhai Naoroji**, the first scientific estimate by **V.K.R.V. Rao**.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- GDP = domestic final output; GNP = GDP + NFIA; NDP = GDP − depreciation; NNP = GNP − depreciation.
- NNP at factor cost = National Income; Per-capita income = National Income ÷ population.
- Market price to factor cost: subtract indirect taxes, add subsidies.
- GDP deflator = (Nominal ÷ Real) × 100; India's base year is 2022-23 (new series Feb 2026).
- Three methods: production/value-added, income, expenditure (C + I + G + (X − M)).
- MoSPI/NSO compiles national accounts; first estimate by Dadabhai Naoroji, scientific by V.K.R.V. Rao.

items.title: Measuring Development — HDI & Inclusive Growth
items.body:
**In one line:** Because income alone does not capture well-being, the UN's Human Development Index scores health, education and living standards together, and 'inclusive growth' asks that the gains reach everyone.

**Why it is asked:** HDI components, India's latest rank and the SDGs are recurring, current-affairs-linked facts.

## Beyond income: the Human Development Index

- **HDI** (UNDP, since 1990) — conceived by **Mahbub-ul-Haq** with **Amartya Sen** — combines three dimensions:
  1. **Health** — life expectancy at birth;
  2. **Education** — mean & expected years of schooling;
  3. **Standard of living** — GNI per capita (PPP).
- India's HDI is about **0.685**, ranked **130 of 193** in the **Human Development Report 2025** — the 'Medium human development' band.

## Related indices

- **IHDI** (Inequality-adjusted HDI), **GDI** (Gender Development Index), **GII** (Gender Inequality Index) and the **MPI** (Multidimensional Poverty Index) capture distribution and deprivation.

## Inclusive & sustainable growth

- **Inclusive growth** — benefits reaching all regions, sectors and social groups; tackles **regional disparities** and **jobless growth**.
- **Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)** — 17 goals adopted by all UN members in **2015**, to be met by **2030**, balancing social, economic and environmental sustainability.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- HDI (UNDP, since 1990) = health + education + standard of living; by Mahbub-ul-Haq and Amartya Sen.
- India's HDI ~0.685, rank 130 of 193 (Human Development Report 2025) — Medium band.
- Related indices: IHDI, GDI, GII, MPI.
- Inclusive growth addresses regional disparities and jobless growth.
- SDGs: 17 goals, adopted 2015, target 2030.

items.title: Achievements & Continuing Challenges since 1947
items.body:
**In one line:** Since 1947 India moved from food shortages to food surpluses and into the world's top-five economies, yet still carries low per-head income, poverty and jobless growth.

**Why it is asked:** A balanced 'achievements and challenges' list is the backbone of essay and short-note answers on the Indian economy.

## Achievements

- **Food self-sufficiency** through the **Green Revolution** — from food imports to buffer stocks and exports.
- A **world-class IT and services** industry and services-export leadership.
- A **large, diversified industrial base** and strong **financial/banking** system.
- Rise to one of the world's largest economies — about **3rd by PPP** and **4th–6th by nominal** GDP, with GDP around **US$4 trillion**.
- Robust **foreign-exchange reserves** and a favourable age structure (**demographic dividend**).

## Continuing challenges

- **Low per-capita income** and persistent **poverty, unemployment and underemployment**.
- **Jobless growth** and dominance of the **informal sector**.
- **Regional disparities** across and within states; rural–urban divide.
- **Low agricultural productivity** despite the sector's large workforce.
- Realising the demographic dividend needs **skilling, health and job creation** — else it risks becoming a burden.

> Nominal vs PPP: India ranks higher on **PPP — Purchasing Power Parity** (GDP valued at what money actually buys at home, which adjusts for lower domestic prices) than on **nominal** GDP (converted to dollars at the market exchange rate). That is why India is 3rd by one measure and lower by the other; per-capita income stays low on both.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- Achievements: Green Revolution food self-sufficiency, IT/services leadership, diversified industry, strong forex reserves.
- India is ~3rd largest by PPP and 4th–6th by nominal GDP (~US$4 trillion).
- Challenges: low per-capita income, poverty, unemployment, jobless growth, informal-sector dominance.
- Regional disparities and low agricultural productivity persist.
- Demographic dividend needs skilling, health and jobs to be realised.

items.title: Black Money Framework & the Andhra Pradesh Economy
items.body:
**In one line:** Black money is income hidden from the tax authorities, which India fights through a cluster of laws and agencies; this note also profiles Andhra Pradesh's largely agrarian economy.

**Why it is asked:** The anti-black-money laws (with their dates and chairs) and AP-specific economic data are directly examinable facts.

## Black money & the anti-black-money framework

- **Black money** = income on which due tax is unpaid, or wealth concealed from authorities; causes include high tax rates, cash-intensive dealings, real-estate under-valuation and the parallel economy. **Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS)** — an **OECD** initiative — aims at curbing tax avoidance by multinational companies that shift profits to low/no-tax jurisdictions.
- **SIT on Black Money (2014)** — constituted in May 2014 on a Supreme Court direction; chaired by **Justice M. B. Shah** (Vice-Chair Justice Arijit Pasayat) to trace undisclosed domestic and foreign wealth.
- **PMLA 2002** (in force **1 July 2005**) — India's principal anti-money-laundering law, it came into force in 2005; the **Enforcement Directorate (ED)** is the agency that investigates offences under it; the **FIU-IND** receives suspicious-transaction reports. Money laundering typically proceeds through three stages: **Placement → Layering → Integration**.
- **Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015** — taxes and penalises undisclosed *foreign* income/assets of residents (distinct from the Benami Act 2016 and the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018).

## The Andhra Pradesh economy — snapshot

| Indicator (latest) | Value |
|---|---|
| GSDP (current prices, projected 2026-27) | ~₹19.75 lakh crore |
| Per-capita income (2024-25) | ~₹2.98 lakh (above national ~₹2.35 lakh) |
| GSVA — primary (agri & allied), 2024-25 | ~37% (well above all-India ~18%) |
| GSVA — industry / services, 2024-25 | ~21% / ~42% |

- AP's primary (agriculture and allied) sector contributes a notably larger share than the all-India average, so AP is distinctively **agrarian-heavy** vs the services-tilted all-India pattern — a leading producer of rice, aquaculture, chillies and tobacco.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- SIT on Black Money (2014) was headed by Justice M. B. Shah, on a Supreme Court direction.
- BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting) is an OECD initiative to curb tax avoidance by multinationals.
- PMLA 2002 (in force 1 Jul 2005) is enforced by the ED; laundering = placement → layering → integration.
- Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) Act, 2015 targets undisclosed foreign wealth of residents.
- AP GSDP (2026-27) ~₹19.75 lakh crore; per-capita income ~₹2.98 lakh, above the national average.
- AP's primary sector (~37% of GSVA, 2024-25) is far larger than the all-India share (~18%); industry ~21%, services ~42%.

items.title: Growth & Development — Approaches, Capital and Thinkers
items.body:
**In one line:** the meaning of "development" changed from "more income per head" (traditional approach) to "more income plus less poverty, inequality and unemployment" (new approach), and capital — physical and human — is the engine behind both.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC 2018 asked when a rise in real GNP does **not** mean development; UPSC 2013 and 2018 asked about capital formation, the capital-output ratio and human capital.

## Two approaches to development

**The story**

| Approach | What development means |
|---|---|
| **Traditional approach** | A **sustained increase in real per capita income**; growth and development are used as **synonyms** |
| **New approach** | Rise in real per capita income over a long period **along with reduction of poverty, inequality and unemployment** — development is **multidimensional** |

- Growth is **quantifiable** — it can be measured in absolute terms (an increase in economic variables over time).
- Development also covers the **composition of output** and the **allocation of resources** to sectors such as agriculture and industry, and needs changes in **social structure, attitudes and institutions**.
- If absolute and per-capita real GNP rise but **poverty and unemployment increase**, there is growth **without** development.

## Capital — the engine of growth

- **Capital formation** (adding to the stock of machines, buildings, infrastructure) is what makes an economy grow.
- **ICOR (Incremental Capital-Output Ratio)** = extra investment ÷ extra output. A **high ICOR** means capital is used inefficiently — a high-saving economy can still grow slowly.
- **Human capital formation** (education, health, skills) raises the **knowledge, skill and capacities** of people — it is **intangible** wealth, unlike tangible physical capital.

## Indices that go beyond income

- **HDI** (Human Development Index), **IHDI** (Inequality-adjusted HDI), **GDI** (Gender Development Index) and the **AHDI** (Augmented HDI, which adds a liberal-democracy dimension) are the indices listed in the source.

## Thinkers on structural change

| Thinker | Idea |
|---|---|
| **A.G.B. Fisher & Colin Clark** | **Three-sector** classification; as income rises, workers move from primary to secondary to tertiary (Fisher-Clark hypothesis) |
| **W. Arthur Lewis** (1954) | **Dual-sector** model — surplus labour moves from the traditional (subsistence) sector to the modern sector |
| **W.W. Rostow** | **Stages of growth** — traditional society, pre-conditions, **take-off**, drive to maturity, high mass consumption |
| **Amartya Sen** | **Capability approach** — "Development as Freedom": expanding the real freedoms people enjoy |

## Don't confuse

- **Physical capital** is tangible (machines, tools); **human capital** is intangible (skills, knowledge).
- A **high** capital-output ratio is bad (more investment per unit of output); a **low** ICOR means efficient capital.

**TL;DR**
- Traditional approach: development = sustained rise in real per capita income (growth and development as synonyms).
- New approach: rise in real per capita income + reduction of poverty, inequality and unemployment (multidimensional).
- Capital formation drives growth; a high ICOR (capital-output ratio) means inefficient capital.
- Human capital formation raises knowledge, skill and capacities — intangible wealth.
- Fisher & Colin Clark: three sectors; Lewis: dual-sector; Rostow: stages incl. take-off; Sen: development as freedom.
keyPoints: Traditional approach: development = sustained increase in real per capita income; growth and development used as synonyms.
New approach: real per capita income rises along with reduction of poverty, inequality and unemployment — multidimensional.
Rising real GNP with rising poverty and unemployment = growth without development (UPSC 2018).
Capital formation drives growth; ICOR = extra investment ÷ extra output — a high ICOR means inefficient capital.
Human capital formation raises knowledge, skill and capacities and adds intangible wealth.
Development indices in the source: HDI, IHDI, GDI and AHDI (Augmented HDI).

items.title: Which Sector Is It? Activities, Collar Jobs & Sunrise Industries
items.body:
**In one line:** an activity's sector depends on what it does — extract from nature (primary), process raw material (secondary) or provide a service (tertiary) — and job "collars" label the kind of work.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC 2024 matched activities to sectors (dairy farm, weaving, storage, mineral exploration); state PSCs ask the collar colours.

## Activity → sector (examiners' favourites)

**The story**

| Activity | Sector | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Dairy farming** | **Primary** | Directly uses livestock and fodder (nature) |
| **Mining / mineral exploration** | **Primary** | Extracts minerals and ores from nature |
| Agriculture, fishing, forestry | Primary | Direct use of soil, water, forests |
| **Weaving cloth** (cotton → yarn, cloth) | **Secondary** | Processes a raw material in a factory or home |
| Sugar mill (sugarcane → sugar, gur) | Secondary | Processing |
| **Construction** (earth, clay → bricks) | Secondary | Manufacturing/industrial activity |
| **Storage** (warehouses, godowns) | **Tertiary** | A service that supports production |
| Transport, communication, banking | Tertiary | Services |
| Call centres, ATM booths, software, internet cafes | Tertiary (modern services) | IT-based services |

- **Historical sequence** in developed countries: primary first → **Industrial Revolution** made the secondary sector dominant → recent decades: the **tertiary (service) sector** dominates.
- The **tertiary sector** produces **no tangible goods**; it aids production. In India it has grown fastest because of the **IT boom, urbanisation** and rising demand for services.

## Collar jobs

| Collar | Kind of work | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Pink-collar** | Caregiving service roles traditionally linked to women | Nursing, daycare |
| **White-collar** | Professional, office work | Accountants, lawyers |
| **Blue-collar** | Manual labour, skilled trades | Electricians, plumbers |
| **Green-collar** | Environment and sustainability jobs | Solar technicians |
| **Grey-collar** | Mix of technical and physical skill | Paramedics, firefighters |
| **Gold-collar** | Highly skilled professionals | Doctors, scientists |
| **Red-collar** | Government and emergency services | Police, government workers |
| **Black-collar** | Hazardous or informal work | Miners, sanitation workers |

- **Sunrise industry** = a sector in its **infancy with high growth potential** (IT, healthcare, telecom, infrastructure, retail).

## Ownership and regulation — examples

- **Organised sector**: government-regulated jobs with job **security**, fixed working hours, pensions and healthcare (government offices, registered companies).
- **GDP across sectors:** only **final goods** and services are counted, to avoid **double** counting of intermediate goods (10,000 kg of wheat at ₹20/kg adds ₹2,00,000).

- **Public sector** (government-owned; objective: **public welfare** and essential services): Indian Railways, public sector banks, Bharat Petroleum.
- **Private sector** (profit objective): Reliance Industries, Tata Group, Infosys, HDFC Bank.
- **Unorganised sector** examples: daily wage labourers, street vendors, small unregistered shops.

## Don't confuse

- **Storage** is **tertiary**, not secondary; **mineral exploration** is **primary**, not tertiary (the two UPSC 2024 traps).
- **Gold-collar** (doctors, scientists) vs **white-collar** (office professionals); **grey-collar** (paramedics) vs **blue-collar** (plumbers).

**TL;DR**
- Dairy farm and mining = primary; weaving and construction = secondary; storage, transport, banking = tertiary.
- Primary → Industrial Revolution (secondary) → service-led (tertiary) is the developed-country sequence.
- Pink = caregiving; white = office; blue = manual; green = environment; grey = paramedics; gold = doctors/scientists; red = police; black = miners.
- Sunrise industry = infant sector with high growth potential.
keyPoints: Dairy farming and mining (mineral exploration) are primary; weaving cloth and construction (bricks) are secondary; storage is tertiary.
Developed-country sequence: primary → secondary (Industrial Revolution) → tertiary (service-led).
Tertiary sector produces no tangible goods; it grew fastest in India due to the IT boom and urbanisation.
Pink-collar = caregiving (nursing); grey-collar = paramedics, firefighters; gold-collar = doctors, scientists.
Red-collar = police, government workers; black-collar = miners, sanitation workers; green-collar = solar technicians.
Sunrise industry = sector in its infancy with high growth potential (IT, healthcare, telecom).

items.title: Index of Eight Core Industries — Weights, Base & Compiler
items.body:
**In one line:** the Index of Eight Core Industries (ICI) is a monthly index of eight infrastructure industries that together make up about 40.27% of the IIP, with refinery products carrying the biggest weight.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC 2012 asked which industries are "core"; UPSC 2015 asked which has the highest weight.

## The eight industries and their weights (base 2011-12)

**The story**

| Rank | Industry | Weight in ICI (%) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Refinery products** | **28.04** |
| 2 | **Electricity** | 19.85 |
| 3 | **Steel** | 17.92 |
| 4 | **Coal** | 10.33 |
| 5 | **Crude oil** | 8.98 |
| 6 | **Natural gas** | 6.88 |
| 7 | **Cement** | 5.37 |
| 8 | **Fertilizers** | **2.63** (lowest) |

- Together the eight carry about **40.27%** of the weight of items in the **IIP** (Index of Industrial Production).
- The ICI is compiled and released **monthly** by the **Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT** (Ministry of Commerce and Industry); the IIP is compiled by the **NSO, MoSPI**.
- It serves as a **lead indicator** of industrial performance, released before the IIP.
- **Textiles, automobiles** and **natural rubber** are **not** core industries.

## Don't confuse

- Under the **current 2011-12 base**, **refinery products** has the highest weight. In the **older 2004-05 series**, **electricity** had the highest weight — which is why the UPSC 2015 key says electricity. Answer by the series the question implies; for current questions, say refinery products.
- **Fertilizers** has the **lowest** weight; it is still a core industry.

**TL;DR**
- Eight core = coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilizers, steel, cement, electricity.
- Combined weight ~40.27% of IIP; refinery products 28.04% (highest), fertilizers 2.63% (lowest).
- Compiled monthly by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT; base 2011-12.
- Textiles is not a core industry.
keyPoints: Eight core industries: coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilizers, steel, cement, electricity.
Combined weight of the eight core industries ≈ 40.27% of the IIP.
Weights (base 2011-12): refinery products 28.04 > electricity 19.85 > steel 17.92 > coal 10.33 > crude oil 8.98 > natural gas 6.88 > cement 5.37 > fertilizers 2.63.
ICI is released monthly by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT; the IIP by NSO (MoSPI).
In the old 2004-05 series electricity had the highest weight (UPSC 2015 key).

items.title: India at a Glance — Current Size, Income Group & Structure
items.body:
**In one line:** India is a lower-middle-income, developing, mixed economy — the 3rd largest by PPP but low on income per head — with most workers still informal.

**Why it is asked:** current-figure questions (rank, size, income group, HDI, informal share) appear every year and are easy marks if the latest numbers are known.

## Headline numbers (latest)

**The story**

| Indicator | Latest value | Source / as of |
|---|---|---|
| Nominal GDP | ~**US$4.06 trillion**, **6th** largest | IMF WEO, April 2026 |
| GDP in terms of Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) | ~US$19.2 trillion — India is the **3rd** largest economy | IMF WEO, April 2026 |
| Per-capita GDP (nominal) | ~**US$2,750** (rank ~149) | IMF, 2026 |
| World Bank income group | **Lower-middle income** | World Bank |
| HDI (HDR 2025) | **0.685**, rank **130 of 193**, Medium | UNDP |
| Informal employment | ~**87%** of workers | ILO, 2025 |
| Agriculture's share of workers | ~**46%** | PLFS 2023-24 |
| Consumption Gini | ~**25.5** (low inequality on consumption) | World Bank |

- India briefly became the **4th largest** economy by nominal GDP in 2025 (overtaking Japan, per NITI Aayog); the IMF's April 2026 dollar ranking places it **6th**. Rankings move with exchange rates — learn both and the source.
- At **independence**, about **70–75%** of the workforce depended on agriculture (NCERT).

## Andhra Pradesh beside the national picture

- AP's GSDP grew about **8%** (constant prices) in **2024-25**, faster than India's **6.5%**.
- AP is India's **largest producer of fish and aquaculture (shrimp)** — a big reason its primary sector is so large.

## Mixed economy and dualism

- **Mixed economy** = **public and private sectors coexist**, with state planning; adopted after 1947 (Industrial Policy Resolutions of **1948** and **1956**), liberalised since **1991**.
- **Economic dualism** = a **modern** sector (IT, organised industry) **coexists** with a **traditional** subsistence sector (small farms, informal trades).
- **Disguised unemployment** — more people work on a farm than are needed; removing them does **not reduce output** (their marginal productivity is zero).

## Don't confuse

- **PPP rank (3rd)** vs **nominal rank (4th–6th)**: PPP adjusts for India's lower prices.
- **Lower-middle income** is the World Bank group by GNI per capita — not "low income".

**TL;DR**
- Nominal GDP ~$4.06 trillion (6th, IMF Apr 2026); 3rd by PPP; per-capita ~$2,750.
- Lower-middle-income economy (World Bank); HDI 0.685, rank 130/193.
- Informal employment ~87%; agriculture ~46% of workers (PLFS 2023-24); ~70–75% at independence.
- Mixed economy = public + private coexist (IPR 1948, 1956); dualism = modern + traditional coexist.
- Disguised unemployment = extra workers whose removal does not reduce output.
keyPoints: Nominal GDP ~US$4.06 trillion — 6th largest (IMF WEO April 2026); 3rd largest by PPP.
India became 4th largest by nominal GDP in 2025 (overtaking Japan, per NITI Aayog).
Per-capita GDP ~US$2,750 (nominal, 2026); World Bank group: lower-middle income.
Informal employment ~87% of workers (ILO 2025); agriculture ~46% of workers (PLFS 2023-24).
At independence about 70–75% of the workforce depended on agriculture.
Mixed economy = public and private sectors coexist (Industrial Policy Resolutions 1948, 1956); liberalised since 1991.
Economic dualism = modern sector coexists with a traditional subsistence sector.
Disguised unemployment: removing the extra workers does not reduce output (zero marginal productivity).

items.title: Black Money — Why It Worries Government & Related Laws
items.body:
**In one line:** black money is unaccounted income hidden from tax; its biggest cost to government is lost tax revenue, and India has layered several laws and bodies against it.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC 2011/2021 asked the main worry about black money; the SIT, PMLA and later laws recur in state PSC papers.

## What and why

- **Black money** = income or wealth on which tax has not been paid, or which is concealed from the authorities — the **parallel economy**.
- **Main worry for the Government of India: loss of revenue to the State Exchequer due to tax evasion** (UPSC answer key).
- Causes: high tax rates, cash-heavy transactions, real-estate under-valuation, corruption.

## The legal and institutional framework

**The story**

| Measure | Year | Point to remember |
|---|---|---|
| **PMLA** (Prevention of Money Laundering Act) | **2002** (in force **1 July 2005**) | Investigated by the **Enforcement Directorate (ED)** |
| **FIU-IND** (Financial Intelligence Unit) | 2004 | Receives **suspicious transaction reports** |
| **SIT on Black Money** | **May 2014** | Chair **Justice M.B. Shah**, Vice-Chair **Justice Arijit Pasayat**; set up on Supreme Court direction |
| **Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act** | **2015** | Taxes undisclosed **foreign** income/assets |
| **Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act** | **2016** | Property held in another person's name |
| **Fugitive Economic Offenders Act** | **2018** | Confiscates property of offenders who flee India |
| **BEPS** (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting) | OECD/G20 project | Stops multinationals shifting profits to low-tax places |

- Money laundering runs in three stages: **Placement → Layering → Integration**.

## Don't confuse

- **Black Money Act 2015** = **foreign** assets; **Benami Act 2016** = property in someone else's name; **FEOA 2018** = offenders who flee.
- **ED** investigates PMLA offences; **FIU-IND** only collects and analyses financial intelligence.

**TL;DR**
- Main worry: loss of revenue to the State Exchequer due to tax evasion.
- PMLA 2002 (in force 1 July 2005) — ED; FIU-IND gets suspicious transaction reports.
- SIT 2014: Justice M.B. Shah (chair), Justice Arijit Pasayat (vice-chair).
- Black Money Act 2015 (foreign assets); Benami Act 2016; Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018.
keyPoints: Main worry of black money for the Government: loss of revenue to the State Exchequer due to tax evasion.
SIT on Black Money (May 2014): chair Justice M.B. Shah, vice-chair Justice Arijit Pasayat.
FIU-IND receives suspicious transaction reports; ED investigates offences under PMLA 2002 (in force 1 July 2005).
Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act 2016 and Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018 complement the Black Money Act 2015.

items.title: For Mains — Characteristics of the Indian Economy & Development
items.body:
This subtopic anchors **Paper-IV (Economy & Development)** questions on India's growth story and its unfinished agenda. Marshal the answer across these dimensions.

| Dimension | Content to deploy |
|---|---|
| **Features** | Lower-middle-income, dualistic, agrarian-employment-heavy, capital-deficient, informal-dominated mixed economy |
| **Growth vs development** | Growth = quantitative; development = +equity/welfare; growth necessary not sufficient |
| **Structural change** | Agriculture → services, weak manufacturing; output–employment mismatch |
| **Challenges** | Jobless growth, regional disparities, informality, low farm productivity, inequality |
| **Way forward** | Labour-intensive manufacturing, skilling, formalisation, inclusive & sustainable growth |

**Data points & authorities to quote:** nominal GDP ~**$4.1 trillion**, **3rd largest by PPP**; GVA shares services ~**55%**, industry ~**28%**, agriculture ~**18%** while agriculture employs ~**45%** of workers; per-capita income ~**$2,750**; **HDI 0.685, rank 130/193 (HDR 2025)**; new **GDP base year 2022-23 (Feb 2026)**; informal workers ~**90%** of the workforce (ILO/e-Shram); Gini ~**25.5**. Thinkers: **Amartya Sen** (capability approach), **Mahbub-ul-Haq** (HDI), **Kuznets / Lewis** (structural change), **Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi** (beyond-GDP).

**AP angle:** AP's GSDP (~**₹19.75 lakh crore**, 2026-27) and per-capita income (~**₹2.98 lakh**, above the national ~₹2.35 lakh) coexist with a **primary sector of ~37% of GSVA** (double the all-India share) — a vivid case of an agrarian-heavy state using the **Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor** and skilling to diversify.

**Use in answers:** (1) open by separating 'growing' from 'developing'; (2) use a **sector-share vs workforce-share bar comparison** as a diagram; (3) cite the HDI rank and the new base-year reform as evidence and 'way forward'; (4) close with Sen's line that development is 'the expansion of real freedoms people enjoy'.
keyPoints: Frame: features → growth-vs-development → structural change → challenges → way forward.
Quote GVA 55/28/18%, agriculture ~45% of jobs, HDI 0.685 rank 130, GDP base year 2022-23.
Key challenge = output–employment mismatch and jobless growth; answer = inclusive, employment-rich growth.
Thinkers: Sen (capabilities), Mahbub-ul-Haq (HDI), Lewis/Kuznets (structural change).
AP angle: agrarian-heavy GSVA + VCIC corridor and skilling to diversify.
